cost/W: Fine-tuning a pretrained network changes all of its weights a little. Take one weight matrix, W, with d rows and k columns: here, a thousand by a thousand.
cost/size: That is a million numbers, all changed, so each new task needs its own copy: another million.
cost/big: By 2021, some pretrained networks had a hundred and seventy five billion weights, and a fully fine-tuned copy for every task was far too costly.
cost/lora: That year, Edward Hu and colleagues at Microsoft proposed LoRA: low-rank adaptation. Adapting means fitting a network to a new task.
cost/idea: LoRA freezes W, and learns only the change, built as the product of two thin matrices: B times A.
cost/rank: B is d by r, and A is r by k. Their thin side, r, is called the rank, and it is small: here, four.
rank/small: To see what r limits, take a small change, five rows by six columns, with r of one. Then B is a single column, and A a single row.
rank/col: Each column of B times A is B times one column of A. Here, that column of A is one number, two, so this column of the change is B's column, doubled.
rank/all: Every column is B's column, stretched, shrunk or flipped by one number. As vectors, they all point along one direction.
rank/two: With r of two, B has two columns, and each column of the change mixes them: some of the first, plus some of the second. Two directions.
rank/def: That count is the rank: how many directions a matrix's columns really use, not counting mixes of the others. B times A never has more than r.
rank/bet: At full size, a thousand columns are all mixed from just four. Hu and colleagues bet that fine-tuning needs only a few directions, and for some tasks, a rank of one was enough.
count/shape: B times A is d by r, times r by k. The inner r's drop out, leaving d by k: W's shape, so it can be added to W.
count/B: Now count what is learned. B has d rows of r numbers: a thousand times four, four thousand.
count/A: A has r rows of k numbers: four times a thousand, four thousand more.
count/total: Together, eight thousand: r times d, plus r times k. That is r times the sum, d plus k.
count/frac: Against the million in W, that is zero point eight percent.
count/wide: Now a W that is not square: two thousand by five hundred. B takes its two thousand rows: eight thousand numbers.
count/wideA: A takes its five hundred columns: two thousand numbers.
count/pct: Ten thousand in all, against the million in W: one percent.
merge/out: While it trains, the layer computes W x, plus B A x. Only B and A learn.
merge/zero: B starts at zero, and A at random. So at first, B A is zero, and the layer gives exactly what the pretrained one did.
merge/start: So training starts from the pretrained network, and moves away only as B learns.
merge/merge: When training is done, add B A into W. The sum has W's shape, so the layer runs exactly as fast as before.
merge/tasks: And each task keeps only its own B and A: eight thousand numbers, beside one shared, frozen W.
